# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Language models routinely act on information they have not written down. A model
completing a rhyming couplet selects its rhyme before it writes the line that ends in it
[@lindsey2025biology; @hanna2026latent]; a model asked for a calculation, or to make a
secret choice and reveal it later, must hold or reconstruct that content across the tokens
it writes in between. How such unwritten information reaches the position that uses it is
a basic question about autoregressive computation, and a practical one. Chain-of-thought
monitoring assumes that the reasoning relevant to a decision passes through, or can be
recovered from, the text the model writes [@korbak2025monitorability;
@baker2025monitoring]. The central risk to that assumption is content that the model uses
but never states [@pfau2024dots; @roger2023steganography; @turpin2023unfaithful;
@chen2025reasoning].

In a transformer, information at one position can reach a later position by three paths
(@fig-overview A). It can be **emitted**: it changes the tokens the model writes, which
are read back as input. It can be **retrieved**: the later position attends directly to
where the information originates, or to visible text from which it can be recomputed. Or
it can be **relayed**: positions of the generated text pick it up and pass it on.
Emitted information is in the text, and retrieved information stays at a fixed position
of the context, where it can be read or probed. Relayed information travels through the
model's own output without appearing in it, so relay is the path by which a model could
hold content across a chain of thought that never states it. A fourth possibility turns
out to matter: a **stored copy**, written once into a structural position of the prompt
next to the source and read directly from there. Prior work shows that planning signals
are decodable ahead of time [@pal2023futurelens; @wu2024plan; @men2024lookahead],
visible in attribution graphs [@lindsey2025biology; @hanna2026latent] and steerable
[@maar2026plan; @ma2026plan; @jacopin2026improvisation]. These methods locate where a
plan is formed or can be changed, not which path it takes to where it is used.

We introduce **route accounting** (@sec-method). A donor's hidden states are written at
the source positions, and the effect is measured where the information is used. Fixing
the generated text separates emission from persistence. Clamping the states of chosen
groups of positions, at every layer, separates direct retrieval of the source from
indirect paths through intermediate positions, which we split by position into the
stored copy, the late lookup just before the target, and relay along the rest of the
generated text. For every group we report interventional sufficiency, necessity and their
interaction. On induction [@olsson2022induction], where the known mechanism passes
information through the position of a copied token, route accounting finds that indirect
path as the largest path in all nine models tested (@sec-control).

Applied to four tasks in 15 checkpoints from three model families, route accounting finds
one principle, within the settings tested (short generated spans, thinking disabled):
**look it up, don't carry it**. Models read unwritten information near the point of use
from a fixed position of the prompt, the source or a copy stored next to it, rather than
relay it along the text they generate (@tbl-map; @sec-lookup). Rhyme plans are read
mainly from the rhyme word (68 to 95% of persistence in all but one configuration), and
relay along the generated line accounts for at most 1% in all 21 runs. Donor states at
every position after a computed value's source move the answer by at most 4.9% (variable
chains) and 6.4% (sums) of the source effect, while written intermediate values are
followed: emission accounts for 83 to 101% of the effect.

Three stress tests, each with a decision rule committed before its result, make relay
useful or the content invisible (@sec-stress). In the Qwen3.5 hybrid, where three of every
four layers can pass information forward only through a recurrent state, a donor signal
entering through the recurrent layers produces 2 to 4% of persistence. When filler moves
line 1 beyond Gemma 3's attention window, Gemma 3 27B shifts toward the stored copy, which
becomes necessary for about half of persistence; the generated text accounts for 9 to 13%,
not split into late lookup and relay, so how much of it is relay remains unresolved. For a
secret choice, pick-specific information is stored at a few low-content prompt tokens and
read at the reveal, and at most 2% of the text-swap effect passes through the intervening
sentence. The one path that grows is the stored copy. It appears at 14B and above in
Qwen3 and at 12B to 27B in Gemma 3, is present in the base checkpoints we tested, and
reconciles published accounts of where the rhyme plan lives [@hanna2026latent;
@lindsey2025biology; @ma2026plan].

**Contributions.** (1) Route accounting, a position-level decomposition of intervention
effects in autoregressive generation into emission, direct retrieval and indirect paths,
with sufficiency, necessity and interaction, validated on a positive control. (2) A
principle with its evidence and scope: in the settings tested, unwritten information is
looked up, not relayed along the generated text, across visible plans, computed values
and hidden choices, families, sizes, prompt formats, instruct and base checkpoints, and
under published feature steering as well as state edits. (3) Three stress tests with
committed decision rules that bound it. (4) A stored copy at the line's final token that
emerges with scale, and a reconciliation of published accounts of rhyme planning.

Where unwritten information travels: the share of the effect by path, as a range over
the models tested, of persistence unless stated. *Looked up*: the target reads the source,
a copy stored at a structural token next to it, or the late lookup. *Relay, or an unsplit
indirect path*: relay along the generated text where it was separated (rhyme plans);
otherwise the named group of intermediate positions. *Visible* content can be recovered by
a reader of the text; *hidden* content cannot. Dashes mark cells the design rules out.
The sections and appendix give the full results with 95% intervals.

:::
